approach: Compare the maximum forward friction with the gravity component along the incline to get the condition, then find each acceleration by adding or removing friction.

steps.text: For the car to speed up while going up, the maximum forward friction the wheels can provide must exceed the gravity component pulling it back down the incline.
steps.equation: condition: μmg cosθ > mg sinθ, so μ > tanθ

steps.text: With this condition met, the maximum acceleration uses the maximum forward friction together with gravity opposing it.
The minimum retardation happens when no friction acts at all, so gravity alone slows the car.
The maximum retardation happens when friction is used fully to brake, adding to gravity instead of opposing it.

final_answer.value: (a) μ > tanθ; (b) a(max) = g(μcosθ − sinθ); (c) a(min retardation) = g sinθ; (d) a(max retardation) = g(sinθ + μcosθ)

common_mistakes.text: Swapping sinθ and cosθ in the maximum acceleration formula gives a(max) = g(μsinθ − cosθ), negative for realistic angles and coefficients, a sign the components were mixed up.
Treating the minimum retardation as zero instead of g sinθ ignores that gravity still acts on the car even when no friction is present.
